title: Erase a Pattern Until None Is Left
statement:
You get two strings, s and part. Repeat this step: find the leftmost place where part appears in s as a contiguous piece, and delete that piece. Stop when part no longer appears anywhere in s.

Return what is left of s (possibly the empty string).

Deleting a piece glues its two neighbours together, and that can create a new copy of part that was not there before.

examples.why: Deleting the inner "ab" leaves "cabd", where a new "ab" has formed. Deleting that gives "cd".
One pass of find-and-delete-all gives "abc", not the answer: the deletion created a fresh copy, which must go too.
part never appears, so nothing is deleted.

constraints: s and part contain only lowercase English letters
hints: Deleting and rescanning from the start works but repeats a lot of work. After a deletion, where can a new copy of part possibly appear?
A new copy can only form right at the seam, which is at the end of what you have built so far if you read s left to right.
Build the answer like a stack: push each character, and whenever the last part.length characters equal part, pop them all.

explain.intuition:
Read s from left to right and build the result as you go, like typing it into an editor. Each time you type a character, check whether the text now ends with part. If it does, press backspace part.length times.

This matches the leftmost-first rule. A copy of part is complete at the moment its last character is typed, and the copy that completes first is the leftmost one still present. After the backspaces, the end of the result is the seam where the neighbours meet, which is exactly where a new copy could form, and the next characters are checked against it automatically.
steps: Keep a stack of characters for the result.
For each character of s, push it.
If the stack has at least m = part.length characters, its last one equals the last of part, and the top m characters spell part, pop m characters.
Join the stack and return it.
pitfalls: Deleting every copy found in one pass and stopping, like the second example. Deletions can create new copies.
Re-searching from the start of the string after every deletion. That is correct but O(n²) on long inputs with many cascades.
Comparing against the top of the stack before it holds at least part.length characters, which reads past the start.

solutions.title: Find, delete, search again
solutions.idea: Do exactly what the statement says: find the leftmost copy, cut it out, repeat.
solutions.time: O(n² / m) in the worst case

solutions.title: Stack of characters
solutions.idea: Push each character; when the top of the stack spells part, pop it off. New copies can only form at the top.

followups: part can be as long as s. How do you avoid the O(m) comparison at each step? (Store a KMP match state with each stacked character.)
Several patterns must be erased at once. Which structure checks the end of the stack against all of them?
